analysis.title: Microsoft Corporation: A closer look at Copilot: a conversation with Copilot EVP, Jacob Andreou
key_insights: BofA hosted an investor group meeting with Jacob Andreou, EVP of Copilot. The discussion covered enterprise AI strategy, how Microsoft differentiates, and where Copilot is going next.

Microsoft's enterprise AI approach rests on model flexibility, predictable costs and business context from the M365 ecosystem. BofA says this supports Copilot paid seat expansion alongside a consumption pricing model.

Microsoft sorts Copilot users into three groups. Starters use limited Copilot features included in existing M365 plans. Subscribers pay for a Copilot seat. Advanced users use modules such as Autopilot and Code and pay for AI consumption.
Microsoft is aiming to lower prices through infrastructure advantages and by adding more AI capabilities to the basic subscription price.
At Ignite, Microsoft introduced 'Today', which helps users prioritize work, and 'Workspaces', where people and agents work together.
Work IQ links Copilot to company data. It is moving from retrieving individual files toward a semantic understanding of work across emails, Teams conversations and documents.

Three stated advantages against AI labs: Work IQ business context, adoption inside existing Office apps without an organization-wide tool change, and Auto mode, which mixes cheaper and more powerful models within one task to control cost.

With paid subscribers on a healthier trajectory, Microsoft is putting more attention on Starter and Advanced users. The aim is to convert Starters to paid seats and to grow consumption revenue from Advanced users.
Advanced users get Cowork (analysis across files), Code (custom apps and dashboards) and Autopilot (background task execution).
Pricing is hybrid. Copilot subscriptions include everyday AI assistance with no consumption charge. Complex workloads are metered and billed on AI consumption.

Longer term, Andreou argues AI should move away from depending on a user's prompt, toward proactive assistance and always-on agents. BofA reads this as steps toward Copilot becoming the central interface for knowledge work.
BofA reiterates a Buy rating and a $630 price objective on MSFT, based on 28x CY27E P/E against a peer range of 18-25x. The stock was $498.30 at publication.

market_movers.rationale: BofA reiterates Buy and sees Microsoft's enterprise AI strategy (model flexibility, predictable costs, M365 context) supporting Copilot paid seat expansion plus consumption pricing.

risk_factors: Near-term gross margin pressure as Azure grows as a share of total revenue.
AI applications and model providers could innovate faster than Microsoft and limit its growth profile.
Enterprise application spending has proven highly cyclical because application projects are discretionary.
